title: Linear Inequalities
tagline: Inequalities in one variable: rules, algebraic solutions and representation on the number line.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ISC Class XI Mathematics syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Syllabus unit and chapter title were taken from the official-verified ISC Mathematics registry entry after the syllabus-aligned rewrite; no board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: An inequality is a statement that one expression is greater than, less than, greater than or equal to, or less than or equal to another. Linear inequalities in one variable are inequalities that can be rearranged into the form ax + b > 0, ax + b < 0, or one of the related forms, with a and b constants. They look a lot like linear equations, but the rules change in one important place: when you multiply or divide by a negative number, the inequality sign reverses. This chapter covers how to solve such inequalities algebraically and how to show their solutions on a number line.

facts.label: Core ideas
facts.value: Inequality symbols; equivalent inequalities; reversal rule for negative multipliers; solution sets in one variable; number-line representation

learningOutcomes: Read and interpret the four basic inequality symbols.
Solve linear inequalities in one variable using algebraic rules.
Remember to reverse the inequality sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number.
Represent the solution of a linear inequality on a number line.
Distinguish between strict inequalities and inclusive inequalities when marking endpoints.

blocks.text: An inequality compares two expressions. The four basic symbols are greater than, less than, greater than or equal to, and less than or equal to. The first two are strict inequalities; the last two are inclusive. A solution of an inequality in one variable is any value of the variable that makes the statement true. A linear inequality in one variable is one that simplifies to a form such as ax + b > 0, where a and b are constants.

items: The four inequality symbols are >, <, >= and <=.
A strict inequality does not allow equality; an inclusive one does.
A solution of an inequality is a value that makes it true.
A linear inequality in one variable simplifies to ax + b > 0 or a related form.

items.text: x > 3 means all numbers strictly greater than 3. x >= 3 means 3 itself is also allowed, along with all larger numbers.
items.note: The difference between > and >= is the single point 3; that single point matters in the final answer.

blocks.text: Solving a linear inequality is very similar to solving a linear equation. You may add or subtract the same quantity from both sides, and that does not change the direction of the inequality. You may multiply or divide both sides by the same positive number, and that also does not change the direction. The one critical rule is that if you multiply or divide by a negative number, you must reverse the inequality sign. Missing that reversal is the most common mistake in this whole chapter.

items: Adding or subtracting the same quantity from both sides keeps the inequality true.
Multiplying or dividing by a positive number keeps the direction.
Multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the direction.
Always simplify to isolate the variable.

items.text: Solve 3x - 5 <= 7. Add 5 to both sides to get 3x <= 12. Divide by the positive number 3 to get x <= 4. Here the sign did not reverse because we divided by a positive.
items.note: The sign only reverses when the multiplier or divisor is negative, so checking the sign of the number you are using is part of the method.

learn.title: Representing solutions on a number line

blocks.text: A number line gives a picture of the solution set. For a strict inequality, use an open circle at the boundary point to show that the point itself is not included. For an inclusive inequality, use a closed circle to show that the boundary point is included. Then shade the part of the line that satisfies the inequality. When the solution is just a single finite interval, shade between the two boundary points and mark each correctly. When it is an unbounded set, shade outward from the boundary point.

items: Open circle: boundary point is not included (strict inequality).
Closed circle: boundary point is included (inclusive inequality).
Shade the region that satisfies the inequality.
Check the endpoint carefully; it is one of the places markers are lost in exams.

items.text: For x > -2, put an open circle at -2 and shade to the right. For x <= 4, put a closed circle at 4 and shade to the left.
items.note: The shading direction depends on the inequality sign, and the circle type depends on whether equality is allowed.

figures.caption: Figure: Number line solutions
figures.description: Two number-line diagrams: one for x > -2 with an open circle and shading to the right, and one for x <= 4 with a closed circle and shading to the left.

keyPoints: A linear inequality in one variable simplifies to a form like ax + b > 0.
Adding or subtracting the same quantity does not change the direction of the inequality.
Multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the direction.
Strict inequalities use an open circle on the number line; inclusive inequalities use a closed circle.
The endpoint of the solution set is one of the most common places to lose marks.
examFocus: Always check whether the inequality is strict or inclusive before drawing the endpoint; a filled circle on a strict inequality, or an open circle on an inclusive one, will be marked wrong.
When you multiply or divide by a negative number, reverse the inequality sign before writing the final answer.

vocabulary.meaning: A statement that one expression is greater than, less than, or related to another by >, <, >= or <=.
An inequality that does not allow equality, using > or <.
An inequality that allows equality, using >= or <=.
The set of all values that make an inequality true.
A diagram used to represent numbers and intervals, including solutions of inequalities.

questions.prompt: When you multiply both sides of an inequality by a negative number, you must:
options: Add the negative number to both sides
questions.explanation: Multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number reverses the direction of the inequality.
questions.commonMistake: Treating a negative multiplier the same as a positive one.

questions.prompt: Which symbol means 'is less than or equal to'?
questions.explanation: <= means less than or equal to, an inclusive inequality.

questions.prompt: Solve -2x + 3 > 7 and state the solution set.
questions.answer: Subtract 3: -2x > 4. Divide by -2 and reverse the sign: x < -2. The solution set is all real numbers less than -2.
questions.explanation: The negative division by -2 reverses the inequality from > to <.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting to reverse the sign when dividing by -2, which would incorrectly give x > -2.

questions.prompt: How do you show x >= -1 on a number line?
questions.answer: Draw a closed circle at -1 and shade the part of the line to the right, showing all numbers greater than or equal to -1.
questions.explanation: The closed circle shows that -1 is included, and the shading shows the direction of the solution set.
questions.commonMistake: Using an open circle for >= and so excluding -1 incorrectly.

questions.prompt: Solve 5 - 3x < 2x + 12. Show your steps and represent the solution on a number line.
questions.answer: Subtract 5 from both sides: -3x < 2x + 7. Subtract 2x: -5x < 7. Divide by -5 and reverse the sign: x > -7/5. Draw an open circle at -7/5 and shade to the right.
questions.explanation: The key step is dividing by -5, which reverses the inequality sign from < to >.
questions.commonMistake: Stopping at -5x < 7 and dividing by -5 without reversing the sign.
